newsitem.title: USA: Dollar closes mixed in U.S. after volatile session.
newsitem.headline: Dollar closes mixed in U.S. after volatile session.

text.p: The dollar ended mixed in the U.S. on Friday, retreating from a fresh 33-month high against the yen and paring sharp early losses against the mark.

Trading centered on the mark, which gyrated after several German officials gave conflicting views on the outlook for domestic interest rates, and the British pound, which rallied on strong U.K. economic performance.

Three Bundesbank officials--council members Ernst Welteke and Olaf Sievert and chief economist Otmar Issing--said they did not see lower German interest rates ahead, but Issing and Welteke also voiced hope that rate cuts were still possible.
The dollar climbed against the mark on the news, since lower German rates would enhance the relative value of assets priced in dollars.

But the subsequent release of a radio interview with Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer, in which he asserted Germany's economy should grow through 1997 without a rate cut, sent the mark soaring against the dollar.

"There were a number of comments out of German authorities as to the interest rate picture and the dollar reacted to every single one of them," said Dennis Pettit, foreign exchange manager at Long-Term Credit Bank of Japan New York.
The dollar closed lower at 1.5205/15 marks from 1.5248/53 at the open, but edged higher to 113.35/45 yen, its highest close since January 1994, from 113.33/38.
Sterling rose to $1.6038/45 from 1.5975/85 at the open after reaching a 15-month peak earlier in the session.
The pound rallied on a report that the British economy grew 0.8 percent in the third quarter, exceeding expectations.
"Britain's economy looks good and people are expecting higher interest rates there," said Dominick Presser, chief dealer at Dresdner Bank in New York.
Meanwhile, the dollar benefited from solid U.S. economic data during New York trading, dealers said.

The Commerce Department reported U.S. durable goods orders rose a robust 4.6 percent in September and the University of Michigan's consumer sentiment index rose to 96.5 in October from 94.7, topping forecasts.
"Those reports need to be picked apart, but they seemed to indicate reasonable growth," said Pettit.
The dollar also continued to rally against the yen, boosted by Japanese investors selling yen to invest in higher-yielding overseas markets.
But the U.S. unit may have reached a near-term peak as it approaches 113.60 yen, the January 1994 high which dealers called a key technical resistance level.
"The dollar has been grinding higher against the yen, and it should continue to do so," Presser said.
In other trading, the dollar fell to 1.2605/15 Swiss francs from 1.2623/28 and fell to Canadian $1.3449/54 from C$1.3459/64. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7900/05 from $0.7925/30.
